7.3.	 FILM AND SCREEN FILM SYSTEMS
visible_text: 17.2.2.3. Detectors based on zero crossing of the second derivative
Imagine a particle crossing an edge in a continuously smooth image, F, moving in a direction orthogonal to the edge (i.e. in the direction of the image gradient). If we plot the gradient magnitude of the image along the path of the particle, we see that at the edge there is a local maximum of the gradient magnitude (Fig. 17.12).
FIG. 17.12. Gradient magnitude at image edges. (a) A detail from the chest CT image from Fig. 17.8. (b) Corresponding gradient magnitude image. (c) A plot of gradient magnitude image across the edge (yellow profile). (d) A plot of gradient magnitude image across the tube-like structure (green profile). The gradient magnitude reaches its maximum at the points where the profiles cross the image edge.
Let us denote the unit vector in the particle’s direction as v, and the point where the particle crosses the edge as x. The gradient magnitude of the image F at x is simply:
∇F(x) = D_v F |x   (17.11)
The gradient magnitude reaches a local maximum at x in the direction v if, and only if:
D_{vv} F = 0  and  D_{vvv} F ≤ 0   (17.12)
Several edge detectors leverage this property. The earliest of these operators is the Marr–Hildreth edge detector. It is based on the fact that the necessary (but not sufficient) condition for Eq. (17.12) is:
D_{xx} F + D_{yy} F = 0   (17.13)
The operator (D_{xx} + D_{yy}) is the Laplacian operator. By finding the set of all points in the image where the Laplacian of the image is zero, we find the superset of all the points that satisfy Eq. (17.12).
visual_relations: Figure 17.12 contains four subfigures: (a) chest CT image detail with yellow/green lines indicating profiles; (b) corresponding gradient magnitude image; (c) 1D plot of gradient magnitude along yellow profile (edge), showing a single peak; (d) 1D plot along green profile (tube-like structure), showing two peaks. The peaks in (c) and (d) align with edge crossings.
units: No explicit units are given; image intensity is dimensionless, spatial coordinates are in pixels, derivatives are per pixel.
uncertainties: Equation (17.13) is stated to be a *necessary but not sufficient* condition for a local maximum of gradient magnitude; thus zero-crossings of the Laplacian include false positives (e.g., saddle points).
summary: This section explains edge detection via zero-crossings of the second directional derivative. It states that at an edge, the gradient magnitude has a local maximum along the gradient direction, requiring first derivative zero and second derivative non-positive (Eq. 17.12). The Marr–Hildreth detector approximates this by using the Laplacian (sum of second partials) zero-crossings (Eq. 17.13), which is necessary but not sufficient. Figure 17.12 visually demonstrates gradient magnitude peaks at edges.

Most frequently, we let G be a Gaussian filter. The Gaussian is infinitely 
differentiable, so it is possible to take an image derivative of any order using this 
approach. The width of the Gaussian is chosen empirically. It determines how 
smooth the interpolation of the digital image is. The more smoothing is applied, 
the less sensitive the derivative function will be to small local changes in image 
intensity. As we will see shortly, this can help us distinguish between the more 
prominent and less prominent edges.
